title: Chicago clubs compared with New York's 52nd Street
summary: About twenty Chicago clubs near the Three Deuces; Chicago rooms were softer and more midwestern than New York cellars.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Can you remember the names of any of the other clubs in that stretch there?

Oh, I'm trying to remember where Eddie South and Billy Taylor were working. They had a trio together. As did Stuff and John Levy. Oh, boy, wait a minute. It was in the area of like the Three Deuces in Chicago, the early Three Deuces, where Art Tatum used to work, and where John Collins worked with Art Tatum for about a year.
And oh boy, I can't remember the clubs.

Now, that's -- oh, boy. Have to chase my memory. Going west. Going west. I'd say about 20. You know. And they were not as concise in structure as the New York 52nd Street thing, because New York, the biggest thing there was the atmosphere and the attitude. They were just a little more -- they were a little more glamorous. I'll put it that way. Because in New York you could walk into the Onyx or the Three Deuces, you're walking into a basement that's been converted into a nightclub.
You know, in a brownstone building, you know?
But in Chicago it was -- they had like soft chairs and a nice meal, that kind of way, you know. It was still the midwest.
But -- well, the stockyards was there. It was easy to get a steak.
